newsitem.title: JAPAN: JGB market ignoring downside risk -- sources.
newsitem.headline: JGB market ignoring downside risk -- sources.

text.p: The downside risk of Japanese government bonds (JGBs) is real, but few players -- especially domestic traders -- seem concerned about that possibility, bond market participants said on Monday.
"Everyone has really become very apathetic about the risk that interest rates may rise," said Shin Nagai, treasurer at ABN AMRO Bank N.V.'s Tokyo branch.
JGBs showed little reaction to a senior Finance Ministry official's comment on Friday that the government bond market is considerably "bubbly", Nagai added.

"If I put it rather harshly, the JGB market is considerably bubbly, and there is the risk of a bursting (of the bubble)," Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, told Reuters on Friday.
"Market players are now satisfied that the Bank of Japan will not be able to raise interest rates in the near term," Nagai said.

However, Nagai said he felt the market's view of the economy was too pessimistic, and added that the BOJ may raise the key official discount rate by 0.5 percentage point and that the key 182nd JGB yield may rise as high as 3.5 percent by the end of the year.
Nagai said the recent surge in JGBs was due to the market's pessimism about the outlook for the economy, and domestic financial institutions' aversion to risk.
"Japanese financial institutions are very sensitive about the risks of investing in the stock market right now," he said.
Once the bad loan problems at Japanese banks begin to recede, such institutions may begin investing in stocks again which may cause a shift away from JGBs, Nagai added.

Foreign players have been more bearish about JGBs than their Japanese counterparts for quite a while, said Jeffrey Young, an economist specialising in economic and market analysis at Salomon Brothers Asia Limited.

Foreign traders seem more concerned about recent rises in inflation than Japanese traders, and seem to be paying more attention to the possibility that short-term interest rates may rise sooner rather than later, Young said.
"A lot of international accounts have been very underweight (in JGBs)... I think a lot of the buying that triggered the recent surge was domestic," he said.
Rumours have circulated in the bond market since the beginning of last week that overseas hedge funds may be behind the recent heavy buying of 123.00 June JGB futures put options, traders said.

They said hedge funds may be buying based on a view that the Bank of Japan may change its current ultra-low interest rate policy before the put options expire on May 30. Most domestic participants expect no such decision by the BOJ before that time.
Foreigners' relative confidence in Japan's economy may be because they place more emphasis on macro-economic indicators, said Masuhisa Kobayashi, fixed-income analyst at Merrill Lynch & Co in Tokyo.

Foreigners seem to find encouragement from Japan's 3.6 percent growth in real GDP last year, and view this as a positive sign for Japan's economy, whereas Japanese market participants seem more concerned with the weakness in business sentiment, which is prompting them to hold relatively bearish views on the economy, Kobayashi said.
The benchmark 182nd JGB yield ended Monday's Tokyo trade at 2.150 percent.
